asOf: USFS Tribal Land Cessions in the United States (2018)
note: Land cessions from Charles C. Royce's schedule 'Indian Land Cessions in the United States' (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), digitised by the US Forest Service with the National Park Service, the EPA and Claudio Saunt (2018). Each shape is one Royce area, dated by its first cession date (treaty, act of Congress or executive order); name = the nation or band as Royce's schedule names it. Areas overlap where land was ceded more than once. Simplified by Orbis.

items.title: Treaty of Greenville
items.text: After their defeat at Fallen Timbers in 1794, the nations of the Northwest Territory ceded most of what became Ohio. The treaty ended the Northwest Indian War.
items.source: Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Greenville'; USFS Royce cessions

items.title: Indian Removal Act
items.text: Congress authorised the President to exchange land west of the Mississippi for the homelands of nations in the East. About 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people were forced west in the years that followed.
items.source: Wikipedia, 'Indian Removal Act' and 'Trail of Tears'

items.title: Treaty of New Echota
items.text: A small Cherokee group signed away the nation's land in the Southeast. The Cherokee National Council never approved it and Principal Chief John Ross did not sign, but the Senate ratified it in 1836.

items.title: The Trail of Tears
items.text: The army began forcibly removing the Cherokee in May 1838. About 4,000 died on the way to Indian Territory, the figure the Cherokee Nation gives; other estimates run to 5,000.
items.source: Wikipedia, 'Trail of Tears' (Cherokee Nation; Oxford Research Encyclopedia of American History)

items.title: End of treaty-making
items.text: The Indian Appropriations Act of 1871 ended treaty-making: from then on, land was taken by acts of Congress and executive orders rather than by treaty.

items.title: The Dawes Act
items.text: The General Allotment Act split reservations into private plots and sold the 'surplus'. Land held by Native Americans fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million in 1934.
